transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A major telecommunications company has announced plans to launch hundreds of low-orbit satellites by 2027 to provide high-speed internet access to remote and rural areas around the world. The company says the satellite network will be able to deliver internet speeds comparable to fiber-optic connections even in the most isolated regions, where traditional broadband infrastructure is either unavailable or prohibitively expensive to build. The project, estimated to cost over 10 billion dollars, aims to connect more than 3 billion people who currently lack reliable internet access. While the initiative has been praised by digital inclusion advocates, it has also faced criticism from astronomers who warn that thousands of additional satellites could interfere with astronomical observations and contribute to the growing problem of space debris. Company representatives say they are working closely with the scientific community to minimize the impact on astronomy and are designing satellites that will automatically deorbit at the end of their operational life.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: Volunteers across the UK are participating in this year's Big Garden Birdwatch, the world's largest wildlife survey. Organized by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, the annual event asks people to spend just one hour counting the birds they see in their gardens or local parks, then submit their observations online. Last year, over half a million people took part, counting more than 8 million birds. The data collected helps scientists track changes in bird populations over time, which provides important information about the health of the environment. This year, conservationists are particularly interested in seeing how house sparrow and starling populations are faring, as these species have experienced significant declines in recent decades. Participants of all ages are welcome to join, and no prior birdwatching experience is necessary—the RSPB website provides identification guides and tips for taking part.
Questions 4 and 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
4. What are volunteers asked to do for the Big Garden Birdwatch?
5. Why are conservationists particularly interested in house sparrows and starlings?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A new community library program in Kenya is helping children in rural villages improve their reading skills while also providing access to thousands of books that would otherwise be unavailable. The program uses donkey-drawn carts that travel from village to village, bringing portable libraries filled with children's books, educational materials, and trained reading tutors. The donkeys can reach areas that are inaccessible to vehicles, making it possible to serve even the most remote communities. Since the program started two years ago, it has served over 20,000 children across 50 villages, and school reading test scores in participating communities have improved by an average of 35 percent. The program's founder says the idea came from watching children share a single tattered textbook in a village school, and she wanted to find an affordable way to bring books to children who needed them. The program is now being expanded to neighboring countries with support from international education organizations.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
6. How does the library program travel between villages?
7. What improvement has been seen in participating communities?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Ella): Hi, Mason. Did you go to the careers fair yesterday? I thought it was really helpful.

Man (Mason): I did go, actually. I was pretty impressed by how many different companies were there. But I'm still not sure what kind of job I want after graduation. I'm a business major, but I don't really want to work in banking or finance like most of my classmates.

Woman: Oh, you don't have to! There were so many different types of companies there. Did you talk to any of the retail management programs? Or the marketing agencies? I remember seeing several tech companies looking for business graduates too.

Man: I did talk to a few marketing agencies, and they sounded interesting, but I'm worried that entry-level marketing jobs don't pay very well at first. I have student loans to pay back, so I need to make a certain amount of money.

Woman: That's a valid concern. But a lot of those companies have good promotion paths—you might start lower, but you can move up pretty quickly if you work hard. Did you talk to anyone in the consulting firms? They usually pay well right out of university, and they hire all kinds of majors.

Man: I walked past the consulting booths, but I was a little intimidated, to be honest. I've heard consulting jobs are really high-pressure with long hours. I want to have some kind of work-life balance.

Woman: That makes sense. I know how you feel—no one wants to work 60-hour weeks all the time. What about the non-profit organizations? There were several there looking for people with business skills to help with operations and fundraising. You might make less money, but the work can be really rewarding.
Man: I actually did stop at one environmental non-profit, and their work really appealed to me. I've always been interested in environmental issues. But again, the starting salary was pretty low.

Woman: You know, a lot of companies—even non-profits—offer student loan repayment assistance now as part of their benefits packages. Did you ask about that? Also, some have professional development programs where they'll pay for you to get an MBA later on.
Man: No, I didn't even think to ask about that! I guess I was just focused on the base salary. I should go back today and talk to them again. The fair is open until 4 PM, right?

Woman: Yeah, it is. I'm actually heading over there in about an hour to talk to a publishing company I missed yesterday. You should come with me, and we can look at the non-profit booths together. Sometimes it's easier to ask questions when you're with someone else.
Man: That sounds great. Let's meet outside the student union at 2 o'clock? I want to do a little research on the organizations first so I know what to ask.

Woman: Hmm, what about the science museum? They have a special interactive exhibit on robots right now that's supposed to be amazing. You can actually control some of the robots and see how they work. It's not just little kids' stuff—I went last month with my roommate, and we had a great time.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The history of the bicycle is a story of continuous innovation spanning over 200 years. The earliest version of the bicycle, known as the "running machine" or "dandy horse," was invented by German baron Karl von Drais in 1817. This early device had no pedals—riders sat astride a wooden frame and pushed themselves along with their feet, similar to how children ride balance bikes today. While it was faster than walking, it never became widely popular because it was difficult to steer and stop.

It wasn't until the 1860s that pedals were added to the front wheel, creating what was called the "velocipede" or "boneshaker"—named for the extremely rough ride it provided on cobblestone streets. These bicycles were made entirely of wood, later with metal tires, and were quite uncomfortable to ride. In the 1870s, the famous "penny-farthing" or "high wheel" bicycle appeared, featuring a huge front wheel and a tiny rear wheel. These could go much faster because of the large wheel size, but they were also dangerous—riders sat high off the ground and could easily tip forward if they hit a bump.

The 1880s saw the development of the "safety bicycle," which looks much like the bicycles we know today. These had two wheels of equal size, pedals connected to the rear wheel by a chain, and eventually inflatable rubber tires that made for a much smoother ride. The safety bicycle was a game-changer because it was accessible to almost everyone, including women, who found the large penny-farthings impossible to ride in Victorian clothing. Bicycles became incredibly popular during the 1890s, in a period known as the "bicycle boom," and they played an important role in the women's emancipation movement by giving women greater mobility and freedom.

In the 20th century, bicycle technology continued to improve with better gears, lighter materials, and more efficient brakes. The last few decades have seen a resurgence in cycling's popularity, driven by concerns about health, traffic congestion, and the environment. Cities around the world are building dedicated cycling infrastructure, and innovations like electric bikes are making cycling accessible to even more people. From its humble beginnings as a wooden running machine, the bicycle has evolved into one of the most efficient, affordable, and environmentally friendly forms of transportation ever invented.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Have you ever wondered why some people seem to make friends effortlessly wherever they go, while others struggle to form close relationships? While personality plays a role, research suggests there are specific habits and behaviors that help people build strong social connections.

First and foremost, good listeners make better friends. People who are skilled at making friends don't spend all their time talking about themselves—they ask genuine questions about the other person and really pay attention to the answers. This doesn't mean you have to be quiet all the time; it means showing curiosity about others and responding thoughtfully to what they say. Studies have shown that people who ask more questions during conversations are better liked by their conversation partners.

Second, being reliable and following through on commitments is crucial for building trust. If you say you'll meet someone at a certain time, be there. If a friend asks for help and you agree to help them, do it. Trust is built through small, consistent actions over time, and people who are dependable naturally attract others because they make people feel secure in the relationship.

Third, successful friendship-builders are willing to be vulnerable and share things about themselves. While you shouldn't overshare too quickly, being open about your own experiences, feelings, and even occasional flaws helps create emotional closeness. People who present a perfect, polished image can seem unapproachable, whereas admitting you're nervous about an exam or that you had a terrible day at work makes you relatable and human.

Fourth, making an effort to stay in touch and nurture relationships is important, especially in our busy modern world. Many friendships fade not because of conflict, but because neither person makes the effort to maintain contact. Sending a quick message to check in, inviting someone to coffee, or remembering small details about their lives and asking about them later all show that you value the relationship.

Finally, being positive and fun to be around helps, though this doesn't mean you have to be happy all the time. People are drawn to those who can see the bright side and who know how to have a good time, even during difficult times. Being supportive when someone is struggling is just as important as celebrating their good news.

The good news is that these skills can be learned and practiced, just like any other skill. If you feel like making friends doesn't come naturally to you, try focusing on one or two of these habits at a time—you might be surprised at how much of a difference it makes.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The United States has no official federal language, though English is by far the most commonly spoken language. However, walk through any major American city, and you'll hear dozens, sometimes even hundreds, of different languages being spoken. This linguistic diversity is not a new phenomenon—it's been part of American life since the country's founding.

Before European colonization, over 300 different Native American languages were spoken across the North American continent. Many of these languages are still spoken today, though most are endangered as younger generations increasingly use English. As waves of immigrants came to the United States from around the world, they brought their languages with them. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, large numbers of German, Italian, Polish, Yiddish, and Chinese speakers arrived in America, establishing ethnic neighborhoods where their native languages were commonly heard.

In the late 20th and early 21st centuries, immigration patterns have shifted, with Spanish becoming the second most spoken language in the country. Today, over 40 million Americans speak Spanish at home, representing about 13 percent of the population. Spanish has such a significant presence in many parts of the country that it's common to see bilingual signs, hear Spanish-language television and radio, and even find government services available in Spanish in many areas.

But Spanish is far from the only language besides English spoken in the US. According to census data, over 350 languages are spoken in American homes. After English and Spanish, the most commonly spoken languages include Chinese (including Mandarin and Cantonese), Tagalog, Vietnamese, Arabic, French, Korean, and Russian. Some cities are particularly linguistically diverse: in Queens, New York, it's estimated that over 130 different languages are spoken, making it one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth.

There has been ongoing debate in American society about language policy. Some people argue that English should be made the official language of the United States to promote national unity, while others believe that linguistic diversity is a national strength that should be celebrated and preserved. Many schools offer bilingual education programs to help English language learners succeed academically while maintaining their native languages, and research shows that being bilingual has cognitive, cultural, and economic benefits in an increasingly globalized world.

23. What percentage of the US population speaks Spanish at home?
